_metadata.description: What health authorities say about intake, as opposed to what regulators have prohibited. This is the evidence that is not an enforcement action, and it exists because a risk scale that can only see enforcement reports "no restrictions found" for sugar and for trans fat alike. Four nutrients: free sugars, sodium, saturated fat, and trans fat's elimination target. REVIEW STATUS: every WHO record here was verified against the published WHO source on 2026-08-24 and quotes it directly; each carries the source URL and a reviewedBy stamp. Records marked 'composition-inferred' quote WHO accurately but apply the guideline to an ingredient WHO does not name — cocoa butter and palm kernel oil — on the basis of their fat composition; WHO names butter, palm oil and coconut oil itself. STILL UNVERIFIED (no reviewedBy): the three JECFA 'ADI not specified' records and the FDA partially-hydrogenated-oils determination. The JECFA evaluations are not machine-readable and the Federal Register blocks automated fetches; both need a person to open the document and quote it.

records.threshold: under 10% of total energy intake, ideally under 5%
records.statement: WHO recommends that "the consumption of free sugars should be limited to less than 10% of total daily energy intake", and that "limiting further to 5% or less of total daily energy intake may provide additional health benefits". Free sugars are "monosaccharides and disaccharides (e.g. sucrose, fructose, glucose) added to foods and beverages by the manufacturer, cook or consumer, and sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, fruit juices and fruit juice concentrates".

records.threshold: elimination from the food supply
records.statement: WHO calls for the elimination of industrially produced trans fat, which "can be eliminated and replaced with healthier fats or oils", and recommends intake of "less than 1% of total energy intake, which is less than 2.2 g per day for a 2000-calorie diet". Partially hydrogenated oils are named as a major source. WHO reports that trans fat intake "increases the risk of death from any cause by 34%, coronary heart disease deaths by 28%, and coronary heart disease by 21%".

citation.title: Trans fat (WHO fact sheet)

records.statement: FDA determined that partially hydrogenated oils are no longer Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) for any use in human food. (Hand-entered: the Federal Register blocks automated retrieval, so this has not been quoted from the source.)

citation.title: Final Determination Regarding Partially Hydrogenated Oils

records.statement: JECFA evaluated citric acid in 1973 and recorded its acceptable daily intake as "NOT LIMITED" — the designation, equivalent to the modern "ADI not specified", used for an additive of very low toxicity where total dietary exposure at the levels needed for its technological effect does not represent a hazard to health.

citation.org: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives
citation.title: JECFA evaluation: citric acid

records.statement: JECFA has allocated Ascorbic acid an ADI "not specified" — the designation used when a substance is of very low toxicity and its intake at the levels needed to achieve the desired technological effect does not represent a hazard to health.

citation.org: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives
citation.title: Evaluations of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)

records.threshold: under 5 g of salt a day, which is under 2 g of sodium
records.statement: WHO recommends adults consume "less than 2000 mg/day of sodium (equivalent to less than 5 g/day salt)", and for children aged 2–15 "adjusting the adult dose downward based on their energy requirements". WHO notes that "the primary health effect associated with diets high in sodium is raised blood pressure which increases the risk of cardiovascular diseases", and that "a significant proportion of sodium in the diet comes from processed foods".

citation.title: Guideline: Sodium intake for adults and children

records.threshold: saturated fat under 10% of total energy intake
records.statement: WHO recommends "no more than 10% of total energy intake coming from saturated fatty acids", and that saturated fat "can be replaced with other nutrients such as polyunsaturated fatty acids, monounsaturated fatty acids from plant sources, or carbohydrates from foods containing naturally occurring dietary fibre". WHO names this among the sources of saturated fat: saturated fatty acids "can be found in fatty meat, dairy foods, and hard fats and oils such as butter, ghee, lard, palm oil and coconut oil".

citation.title: Saturated fatty acid and trans-fatty acid intake for adults and children: WHO guideline
